sections.title: 1. Scheduling a Deferred One-Time Job — at

content.text: A deferred task is something that should run once, in the future, and then be done. Think: "remind the on-call engineer at 6am" or "apply this firewall change tonight during the maintenance window." The at command is built exactly for this.
You give at a TIMESPEC, then type the commands you want to run, then press Ctrl+D to finish. Or, more reliably, redirect a script file in as input instead of typing interactively.

✗ COMMON MISTAKE Typing commands interactively and forgetting Ctrl+D — the job just sits there waiting for more input and never gets scheduled. When scripting or automating this, always redirect from a file instead: at TIMESPEC < script.sh.
List pending jobs for the current user
Show the exact commands and environment a job will run with
Cancel a scheduled job before it runs

🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL Unprivileged users can only see and manage their own at jobs. root can see and manage everyone's. If a job you scheduled as your own user isn't showing up when someone else checks atq, that's expected behavior, not a bug.
A recurring job runs on a repeating schedule instead of once. crontab -e opens your personal crontab in an editor (Vim by default) where you define these jobs.
# | | | | .---- day of week (0 - 6) (Sunday=0 or 7) OR sun,mon,tue ...
An exact value (5th minute, 5th day, etc.)
A list — can mix in ranges too, e.g. 5,10-13,17
Every x units — */15 in minutes = every 15 minutes

🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL If BOTH day-of-month and day-of-week are set to something other than *, the job runs when EITHER condition is true — not when both are true. This is a classic exam trap: 15 12 15 * Fri some-command runs on the 15th of the month AND every Friday at 12:15, not only when the 15th falls on a Friday.
*/5 9-16 * Jul 5 echo "Chime" # every 5 min, 9am-4:59pm, every Fri in July

✗ COMMON MISTAKE Assuming 9-16 in the hours field means "until 4pm sharp." It actually means the job window runs through the entire 16th hour — so with a */5 minute interval, the last run is at 16:55, not 16:00.
System-wide recurring jobs (as opposed to a single user's personal crontab) should never be edited directly in /etc/crontab. Best practice: drop a custom file into /etc/cron.d/ instead.

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS If a package update ever overwrites /etc/crontab, anything you added directly to that file is gone. A file you placed in /etc/cron.d/ survives that update untouched. This is the same 'never edit the vendor file directly' principle you'll see again with systemd unit files and tmpfiles.d.
System crontab format — one extra field
System crontab entries add a user field between the time fields and the command — because the system needs to know which account should run the job.
# minute hour day month weekday user-name command
Custom crontab files (your preferred place for new system jobs)
Executable shell scripts (not crontab files) — run via run-parts
Ensures important periodic jobs still run even if the system was off when they were due
⚠ WARNING Scripts placed in the cron.hourly/daily/weekly/monthly directories must be executable (chmod +x) or run-parts silently skips them — no error, they just never run.

🔎 REAL-WORLD EXTENSION /etc/anacrontab uses a different 4-field format entirely: period-in-days, delay-in-minutes, job-identifier, command. Its whole purpose is catching up on jobs a normal cron schedule would have silently skipped if the machine was powered off.
systemd timers — the modern alternative to cron
A systemd timer unit activates a matching service unit on a schedule. Timers integrate with journald logging and systemd's dependency system, which makes them easier to debug than a silent cron job.
Description=Run system activity accounting tool every 10 minutes
Absolute schedule, cron-like but more readable — *:00/10 = every 10 minutes
Relative to boot time — OnBootSec=15min fires 15 minutes after boot
Relative to the last activation — fires again N time after the last run

🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL Never edit unit files under /usr/lib/systemd/system directly — a package update will overwrite your changes. Copy the file to /etc/systemd/system/ first, edit the copy, then run systemctl daemon-reload. Files in /etc/systemd/system/ always win over identically-named files in /usr/lib/systemd/system/.

Temporary directories and volatile runtime files (much of /run, /tmp) need to be created on boot and periodically purged so they don't fill the disk with stale data. systemd-tmpfiles handles both jobs from declarative config files instead of ad-hoc cleanup scripts.
Seven columns: Type, Path, Mode, UID, GID, Age, Argument.
Create a directory if missing (not auto-purged)
Create a directory if missing; empty it if it exists
Recursively restore SELinux context, permissions, and ownership

The first line creates /run/systemd/seats if missing and never purges it. The second creates /home/student, empties it if it exists, and during a --clean run removes anything untouched for more than a day. The third creates a symlink and never purges it.
Where the config lives — and which one wins
Runs automatically at boot via systemd-tmpfiles-setup
Purges anything past its configured max age; runs on a timer (systemd-tmpfiles-clean.timer)
